I was pointing out that small industries in one part of Canada are more likely to be favoured under this legislation than are small industries in other parts of Canada, unless some regard is given to taxation.
I draw this statement to the attention of hon. members, because I believe it crystallizes what I have been saying. Mr. K. A. Christie, K.C., vice-chairman of the Hydro Electric Power Commission, told the Toronto board of control that the hydro would not be able to continue as a public utility without this advantage of tax exemption. That is a frank admission of an important truth. If power development in one section of Canada is relieved of taxation, both federal and provincial, the advantage to industries using it is obvious.
I urge that for the bank to succeed in rendering that assistance which it should render to small industry-and in this respect I suggest the bill is defective-some regard will have to be had to the suggestion that there be some geographical considerations as to where this assistance can be applied. As other hon. members have pointed out, it would be just too bad if the industrial development bank were to look at the industrial field in Ontario and Quebec, and say, "It is in those provinces that small industries are more likely to succeed. We are going to have a greater population in those centres, so, perforce, it is in those provinces that the assistance will be given by the bank. Power is cheaper, because the power producer pays no provincial or federal taxes. On the other hand, in the other provinces of Canada every user of electricity must pay more, because it is bought from a private corporation which does pay taxes to the municipal, provincial and federal authorities."
I, too, share some misgivings in connection with putting the federal treasury into the banking business. It is really not the banking business, and I think the fact that the bill has been referred to as one setting up an industrial bank has created a wrong impression in the minds of most people. The organization proposed is really a loan company, and its opera-

Industrial Development Bank
tions will be more analogous to those of a loan company than to those of a bank, as we understand banking.
I should like to think of this institution, as a pontoon bridge, a temporary auxiliary structure designed purely and simply to get us back from a war-time to a peace-time economy; that it will have served that purpose, within the five, ten or fifteen post-war years during which we shall pass from a war-time to a peace-time economy, and the need for government assistance will have passed out of existence, because in the meantime private enterprise and private industry will have caught up with the normal needs. As a matter of fact, I believe the fact that this bill is deemed desirable and necessary is a criticism of our private banks, loans companies and insurance companies, owing to the fact that they have not seen the necessity and desirability of setting up some such institution as is contemplated in the bill.
There is now, and -there will be in even greater volume when the war is over, a tremendous amount of money looking for investment. The era of employment to which we all look forward can come about only to the degree to which industry becomes active and alert. I would hope, and I would certainly think the government would hope that there might be a rapid conversion of victory bonds in order that the money represented thereby might find its way into industry for the production of consumer and capital goods. So far as I can see, it is only in that way that we can ever have that era of industrial prosperity we all desire so much.
It is for that reason that I for one favour the bill, and in that I believe the people of Alberta will support me. I suggest, however, that the committee should give serious consideration to some direction as to where and how the loans of -the bank are to be allocated. We must visualize the diversification of industry, and that can be brought about only if the men who are doing the lending view Canada as a whole, see the potential industrial future of the whole country, and give some thought to developing new industry in new areas.
The fact that we have no dye or chemical industry, and that we have never had one, is a trite commentary on our Canadian economic policy. Surely with the reserves of coal we have in Canada we should never again be as dependent as we have been upon Europe and other countries. I would hope that the directorate of the bank would envision a broad and diversified industrial development, so that we might give a start to those industries which bid fair to operate successfully in Canada.
One of the things which has come out of this war and of which I am very proud is the nitrogen plant located at Calgary. For the first time this chemical is being produced in Canada as an industry in itself. I am reliably informed that the Calgary plant is one of the most economically and efficient producers of ammonia nitrate, the base for all explosives, to be found anywhere in the world. Thanks to the engineering and scientific ability of our own Canadians a way has recently been found of pelleting ammonia nitrate, and this can now be used as a fertilizer. A few months ago we were shipping this chemical to five or six different explosive plants in the United States, but now the same product is being shipped in the form of fertilizer to at least four different countries.
I hope that the board- of this bank keeps in mind not only the diversification of existing industry but the sponsoring and assisting of new industries, of which we have all -too few in this country.

Mr. Speaker, there have been a good many matters raised in this debate, many of them relevant to the bill which is under discussion and some of them not quite so relevant.
At the outset of my remarks I wish to refer to certain statements made by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Bla-ckmore) which fall under the second category and which relate to the price and supply of sugar, which, as the house is aware, falls under the department with which I have the honour to be associated. Speaking in the debate last Tuesday, March 7, he made this statement, as reported in Hansard at page 1278:
I believe, solemnly that there has been no need of scarcity of sugar in Canada during this war, or for the years immediately preceding the war, nor has there been any reason or justification for the high prices of sugar which have prevailed. Evidence which I adduced the other night proved conclusively the soundness of my position. I believe that quantity and price have been affected, not so much iby the circumstances of war, as by the fact that prior to the war and also during the war the production and sale of sugar have been manipulated by a sugar trust or combine and that one of the dominating units in this trust has been the St. Lawrence Sugar Refining Company.
I find it hard to imagine a statement of comparable length which could contain, a greater number of errors and inconsistencies.
Industrial Development Bank

Let us see what the facts are on this question. The hon. member alleges, first, that there was a scarcity of sugar immediately preceding the war, and the fact is that there was no shortage of sugar immediately preceding the war. On the contrary, there had been a huge surplus of sugar overhanging the world market for many years. Then he went on tc say:
. . . nor has there been any reason or justification for the high prices of sugar which have prevailed.
Before the war, in fact during the whole period from 1920 to 1939, the price of sugar was not high as he says, but was consistently lower than in any previous time in history.
Coming now to the period of the war itself, just think of the difference in the way in which sugar was dealt with in this war and in the last. In the last war the government did not take any effective action to control prices and the price of sugar went as high as twenty-five cents a pound. With that experience in mind, the government in this war at the very outset took appropriate steps to control the distribution and to control stocks. As a consequence of the measures which were taken there was no shortage of sugar in Canada until rationing was adopted in February, 1942, and the price of sugar has increased to only about eight and one-half cents a pound.

speechtext:
I should now like to turn to the provisions of the bill which is under discussion.
As I said at the outset, a good many points of substance have been raised in connection with this measure and, as some of the hon. members who raised them have indicated, I feel that a good many of these points can be more appropriately dealt with when the bill is before the banking and commerce committee. A good many of them involve questions that are perhaps of a rather technical or detailed nature, and the committee will probably want to call evidence in order to obtain the benefit of specialized views on these questions. However, there have been a considerable number of suggestions and criticisms involving matters of principle, and with these I should like to deal briefly in my remarks in closing the debate.
The first point is.the need for the proposed bank. The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) and the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) in particular have suggested that in my opening remarks I failed to demonstrate the need for such an institution. I thought I had, and that thought has been rather borne out by the majority of the speeches which have been made on the second reading. The majority of hon. members who have spoken seem to feel that there is a definite need for an institution of this kind. I am convinced that there is, and, if I may, I should like to illustrate that need by a concrete example.
Take the case of an individual or a group of individuals contemplating the establishment of a small or medium-sized industry, say a plastic industry such as was suggested by the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia (Mr. Mayhew) this afternoon. These people have $25,000 of their own capital. The enterprise they have in mind would require an investment of, say $50,000 to put up the plant, equip it with machinery and so on, and in addition to that they require $10,000 or $15,000 for working capital to purchase raw materials and pay wages until the product is sold. If they had $50,000, if they had the plant constructed and in operation, there is no doubt in the world that the existing commercial banks of the country would be ready and willing to make them that working capital loan of $10,000 or $15,000 to which I have referred. The difficulty they face is to get a loan of $25,000 to enable them to build a plant.
I know the experience of my hon. friend the member for York-Sunbury is greater than my
Industrial Development Bank

own. However, I have practised law in one of the largest industrial centres of Canada for over twenty years. In the course of that time I have acquired some knowledge of the financial problems of industrial enterprises, both large and small, and I know, and I believe the hon. member for York-Sunbury knows, that it would be extremely difficult for an enterprise of that kind to get that $25,000 to enable it to construct and equip that plant. There would be only two sources from which they could get it. They might possibly get it from one of the mortgage institutions, although as a rule life insurance and mortgage companies do not like to lend for five, ten, or fifteen years on mortgages on industrial property. They might get it from a private lender, but under those circumstances, I fancy, speaking from my own experience, they would probably have to pay a high price for the money.
I am satisfied, therefore, that in such a case -and I think it is perhaps fair to say that it is typical of the small or medium-sized industries which this bank is designed to assist-* there would be no readily available credit agency from which that credit of $25,000 could be obtained; and yet the enterprise might be a perfectly sound one, quite likely to succeed, with competent management and all the rest.
The purpose of this bank is not, as some hon. members have suggested, to make obviously bad loans but to supplement the operations of existing lending institutions. It is not intended to compete, nor do I believe that it will compete, with existing chartered banks. It does not extend government ownership or control over those banks, and it does not encroach upon their operations in any way which in my view might undermine their earning power or their independence.
Incidentally, I was rather puzzled in listening to the hon. member for York-Sunbury and the hon, member for Rosedale when they expressed the view that existing credit institutions were entirely capable of taking care of intermediate or long-term credit for small industries in cases such as I have outlined, and particularly so because the day before the hon. member for York-Sunbury made his speech with reference to this bill I read in the Ottawa Journal what I assumed to be the latest supplementary programme of the Progressive Conservative party, of which he is such a distinguished member, and I noticed item five of the suggested programme recommending "consideration of the establishment of a central farm bank to operate in cooperation with private lending institutions."
I find it a little difficult to see why the credit requirements of agriculture should be so differ-

ent from those of industry that they should require a government central farm bank to operate in cooperation with private lending institutions. I cannot help having a shrewd suspicion that if it had not been indicated in the speech from the throne that the government proposed to introduce legislation to create an industrial development bank we might not have seen a suggestion of that kind in one of these supplementary programmes. Be that as it may, I find a certain inconsistency between the suggestion contained in that proposed platform and the criticism which was offered, particularly by the hon. member for Rosedale.
The second point I should like to deal with relates to the scope of the bill. There has been a considerable amount of discussion of that feature. I simply wish to point out that loans will be made to industrial enterprises as defined in the bill; it is the type of business engaged in which is the limiting factor, and there is no intention to limit the operation of the measure by reference to the class of persons engaging in that business. The point was raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) as to whether it would be available to cooperative enterprises. My own view is that it would. I do not know what the legal situation would be. I assume they are able to incur obligations, and I do not see why a cooperative carrying on industrial enterprises of the nature contemplated in this bill would not be eligible for credit under the proposed legislation.
I do not want to discuss detailed matters. They can be more appropriately dealt with before the committee. However, the question was raised as to assistance to mining. In that connection I would say that the facilities of the bank will be available to a mining enterprise which was in that stage of production; that is to say, if the mine wished financial assistance to build a smelter or a processing plant in order to process ore, then it would come within the definition of an industrial enterprise. On the other hand, the bill does not contemplate and would not permit loans to prospecting mining companies, and in my view I think it would be most undesirable for an institution of this kind-

There is a good deal to be said for that suggestion, but in answer to the criticism I would say that the government considers that, whatever other credit legislation may be adopted, the creation of an industrial development bank of the nature provided for in this bill will be necessary in any event. It is a new institution. It will require a certain amount of time to organize, and it was felt that the bill for the creation of this bank being ready it was desirable to place it before parliament as soon as possible in order that parliament might discuss it and the banking and commerce committee discuss it. It was thought that was preferable to bringing down the Industrial Development bank bill, the Bank Act and other bills which may be introduced. Certainly they could not all be discussed at the same time. There may be some merit in the suggestion that they should have been brought down at the same time, but I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is not really a very serious objection, and that parliament and the country would probably be just as well served by this bill being introduced first and the members being given the opportunity, as they have been given, to debate it now and have it referred to the banking and commerce committee for detailed discussion there.
The next point which was raised along general lines was that capital resources of this bank are inadequate for the purposes which it is designed to serve. Here again, I wish to emphasize the point that this bank is only supplementary to existing credit agencies. It is not intended that this bank should provide all the industrial credit that is needed in this country. The larger enterprises, the larger concerns, which have been able to rely in the past on the investment market by making public issues of preferred stocks and bonds, may and should continue to avail themselves of that market. It is anticipated that they will do so. The comparisons that have been made with the increased national income are, I suggest, completely misleading, and as a final point on this question of the adequacy or otherwise it was felt that parliament might well object to creating what, for want of a better term, I may describe as an open-end credit institution. Just in passing I might [DOT]state that prior to the war the industrial loans of the chartered banks averaged somewhere in the vicinity of $200,000,000. I cite that figure simply to give the house some idea that an institution with lending resources of $100,000,000 is not merely a drop in the bucket as some hon. members appear to believe.
There is also this further point. It is felt, and I believe rightly so, that the influence of this bank may well be greater than the
amount of its own resources, and the very fact that the industrial development bank is willing to participate in an industrial enterprise may well encourage others to put in capital as well.
Finally, there is the point touched on by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) this afternoon, namely, if $100,000,000 proves inadequate it is open to parliament to amend the bill and to increase the permissible amount of loanable funds. There was objection taken to the association of this industrial bank with the Bank of Canada, our central bank. It is perfectly true, as the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) and others have indicated, that the primary function of a central bank is to control the volume of money and credit in the country. But that fact does not preclude a central bank either directly or through a subsidiary, as in this case, from engaging in lending operations of a special character. There is ample precedent for that in the central banks of other countries. For instance, the federal reserve bank in the United States makes loans under section 13 (B) of the Federal Reserve Act. The Bankers' Industrial Development Company, to which the hon. member for Rosedale referred this afternoon, was set up under the auspices of the Bank of England, and I am advised that the central banks of other countries do engage in lending of a special character.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Bur-rard also raised the point that if this bank commences its operations with $100,000,000 of Bank of Canada money, which in the ordinary course would go out into the commercial banking system of the country, it would enable the chartered banks, the commercial banks, to expand their loans and deposits by some $2,000,000,000. While that is perfectly true in theory, of course, it would only happen if the Bank of Canada saw fit to allow this to take place. The chartered banks would be in a position to expand their deposits and their loans only to the extent suggested by my hon. friend if the Bank of Canada failed to take appropriate action. The Bank of Canada controls the reserves of the chartered banks. It is buying and selling securities every day for the purpose of increasing or decreasing those reserves, and the amount involved here would cause no difficulty whatever so far as controlling the reserves of the chartered banks is concerned.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the question was raised that the creation of this bank was an undesirable encroachment on the field of private enterprise; that it was a field which private enterprise was quite capable of filling, and that consequently it should be left with private

enterprise to make loans of this kind. As to that, I suggest that in the past private enterprise in this country has not, for very good reasons, mind you, made the intermediate loans or long term loans of the nature contemplated in this bill.

I would say the principal reasons are, as I indicated in my opening statement on the bill, that their liabilities are entirely or largely of a demand nature or of a very short term nature, and that consequently the type of credit which our banking system contemplates they should extend is credit which will be for a year or not much longer than a year. Our banks, and I think quite properly so, have never gone into the longterm lending field, lending of the type I have described in the example I gave at the outset of my remarks. I feel that they quite properly have not gone into that field, and I think the wisdom of that course was demonstrated during the period from 1930 to 1935 or 1936 when banks in other countries ran into serious difficulties as a result of following a different policy.
The question of public ownership of certain enterprises is, of course, a moot one. My own view is that public ownership is omty a means to an end. It is not an end in itself, and it is justified in those cases, but those cases only, where we have a policy that we wish to be carried out and where we believe that that policy can best be achieved by public ownership.

I should like to conclude my remarks, which I hope have not been too long, by quoting from a speech made by Mr. Churchill a little over

two years ago, in which I entirely concur. He was speaking in the Guildhall on March 21, 1942, and said:
The modern state will increasingly concern itself with the economic well-being of the nation, but it is all the more vital to revive at the earliest moment widespread, healthy and vigorous enterprise, without which we shall never be able to provide in the years when it is needed the employment for our soldiers, sailors and airmen to which they are entitled after their duty has been done.
And a little later in his speech he said:
And I tell you my solemn belief, which is that if we act with comradeship and loyalty to our country and to one another, and if we can make state enterprise and free enterprise both serve national interests and pull the national wagon side by side, then there is no need for us to run into that horrible devastating slump or into that squalid epoch of bickering and confusion which mocked and squandered the hard won victory which we gained a quarter of a century ago.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
In the statement the minister made the other evening he covered almost every phase of this subject and left very little for a member of the opposition to say. I believe the record of Ontario and of Toronto has been most creditable as far as the navy is concerned, with 2,044 officers and 29,958 ratings enlisting in that province and city. Starting from scratch the navy, the senior service, has written a glorious page in the history of courage in this war, and I believe a great deal of the credit for the showing made by the navy in the Toronto district is due to the work which was done by the city itself, the harbour commission and the schools. I was a member of the Toronto harbour board when it was first formed, before the Navy League was formed, and the city of Toronto was very generous in helping the senior branch of the service with grants of all kinds and tag days. I remember when there was no navy

War Appropriation-Naval Services
league, when the sea cadets carried on the work; I can also remember when there was a navy league, which sometimes between the two wars went to sleep on the job. I was glad to hear the minister give credit to the work done by the sea cadets, who were largely instrumental in bringing so many men into the naval service and merchant marine.
The reclamation work in the harbour of Toronto covered twelve or thirteen miles of waterfront; and notwithstanding what was said the other evening, a great deal of that work to aid the senior service was done by the public bodies I have mentioned and by the rowing clubs, the canoe clubs, the swimming clubs and the small yacht clubs; not the larger clubs, which were not much interested at the time. From 1923 on, splendid work in connection with the navy was done by Commander Hose, who had a great deal to do with putting the naval service on its present basis. At one time the navy had a boathouse at the western end of the harbour, at Hanlon's point; then the old steamer Cambria was given to them, and it was kept at the foot of York street before the waterfront improvements were begun in 1913. With the coming of the viaduct it was necessary for us to move the various aquatic clubs out to Sunnyside, and after that the navy work was carried on with the assistance of grants from the city of Toronto and tag days held by the Navy League, and so on. I want to make a fair statement of the case,' and I shall take only a few moments to do so.
Shortly after the war we were visited by three admirals of the fleet. The first to come was Admiral Jellicoe, in December, 1919. I showed him the old quarters of the sea cadets and the naval volunteers. Later on we had a visit from Admiral Beatty, Admiral of the Fleet, and the third to visit us was Admiral Tyrwhitt. The work of the Navy League in Toronto was greatly aided by regattas and tag days held by it. I was glad to see the minister at the Canadian Henley last year. We had the Dominion day regatta, the high school regatta, the canoe regatta, the swimming regattas, the Canadian Henley, and finally the exhibition regatta in the fall. We also had a visit by Mr. Peter Wright, president of the British seamen's union, who came to urge that something should be done for the merchant marine of this country. I well remember in this house, when I was calling attention to the necessity for rearmament on land, on sea and in the air, for many years before the present war broke out, and between the two wars, that when there were several disasters on the great lakes I suggested
advancing the grain crop from the head of the lakes, ships were wrecked, and we had no proper merchant marine service on the lakes or aids to navigation to take care of those men. Many of them were drowned, and all they could do was blow a whistle, in the hope that they would attract the attention of some United States life-saving station in order that their lives might be saved. That showed the length, depth and breadth to which disarmament and pacifism had gone in this country.
In my opinion the statement made by the minister is a most commendable one, because we must realize that the sea is our life. This empire came into being by the sea, and cannot exist without it. But between the two wars disarmament and the reduction of our sea power had its effect. As I have said on many occasions when speaking in that period between the two wars, I have been opposed to the absolute complacency of parliament in not having paid more attention to this matter. It has been stated in our financial statements that at one time we were the fifth trading nation of the world. I pointed out that we had no fleet, with the exception of the merchant marine, and that that merchant marine was doing good work on the oceans and the seas, and in the inland waterways of Canada. As I said, at a most critical time nothing was done about it.
In 1937 I urged a vast shipbuilding policy for Canada and the empire. The imperial conference was about to be held in London, and it will be remembered that New Zealand and Australia asked for a vast empire shipping and air scheme, not only to look after conditions at that time, but to prepare for what was believed to be an approaching war. Canada said, " We have no commitments," and that parliament would decide. We missed one of the greatest opportunities at that conference to prepare for this war and to join in the work. I have always laid stress on the importance of our merchant marine for the defence of Great Britain-and not only Great Britain, but the whole empire. I have called attention to this fact on many occasions when speaking in the house. I have asked about the inability of the British merchant marine and empire to retain the commercial supremacy they had for 150 years, without increased votes and without looking after the merchant marine.
The merchant sailors got very little help. I have seen steamers leave Toronto, many of them without proper crews. All they could do was pick up some stragglers on the docks. I was glad to hear the minister's announcement the other night with respect to the sea cadet movement, which is preparing a way not only

War Appropriation-Naval Services
for the present war but for the merchant marine trade war which will follow. The sea cadets are being trained so that when they take their places in any ship of any size, either on the oceans or on the inland waterways of Canada, they will be found helpful. This is a most commendable feature. I saw something of them at the Royal Canadian Henley. I was glad to see the minister there, and to note the interest he has taken in this particular branch of the work of his department. It is the most important of all.
Before the days of Munich, in 1934, 1935, 1936 and 1937, I urged in the house that we should do something for those who were riding the rods, young men who were coming out of high schools, numbering about 250,000 each year. I proposed in the debates of those days that instead of spending a billion dollars on the dole, as was done by the municipalities, provinces and the federal authorities, we should do something for those young people. In that I was borne out by my late friend, Mr. Rogers. I took that stand, realizing that since the days of the Nile rebellion we have been an aquatic people. It will be recalled that during the General Gordon trouble in the Nile river they had to send to Ontario and Quebec, to the lumber camps, to get men to navigate the rapids. For many years before the war I urged in the house that we should have a naval policy, a grant to Singapore base, and should have adopted the Jellico report for the pacific. We should have had a vast shipbuilding policy, and in addition to that we should have gone into some sort of educational system by which we would have taken the young people who were riding the rods in the days of depression and given them an opportunity to learn trades and have a military training. At the end of three years, after having served their apprenticeship, they would have been ready to man any ships on the lakes or the oceans. Had we followed that suggestion, not only on the sea but on the land and in the air we would have had at least 25,000 skilled pilots and air mechanics, and at the outbreak of war we would not have had as much trouble.
I am glad to see that provision is being made for the future, because, when the war is over-and there is no doubt about this at all-Canada will have to maintain a large army, navy and air force for many years to come. There should be a future for the young people who are coming out of the high schools and universities to-day, and entering the navy. There should be some future occupation for them,- and they should be able to accept naval service as their profession; because, if we are to hold our own in the days that are to come, both in war and after the
[Mr. Church,[
peace is won, we shall have to do something to maintain our position as a great trading nation on the seas.
The Book of Common Prayer-it is not often read in the house-does contain two prayers which the rubric directs shall be read and used twice a day by those in His Majesty's navy. In one of those prayers the officers and men pray that they may be a safeguard unto our Most Gracious Sovereign Lord King George, and His Dominions, and be security for such as pass upon the seas, upon their lawful occasions. I direct attention to the last few words, "upon their lawful occasions", because they describe most eloquently the true function of the whole fleet, and the duty of the navy. It means that it has a duty in peace and war, one which is realized by all who serve in it, from the ratings to the top, to establish and maintain order, justice and freedom in the world; for sea power is not an instrument of tyranny; it is anti-tyrannous. It does not seek domination, but offers freedom for all those who pursue their lawful occasions, as it is set out in the Book of Common Prayer. So that I believe the minister, in the step he has taken, has fulfilled the object of that particular work.
In 1793, during the darkest hour of the war with Napoleon, Pitt referred to the drawing forward of many domestic matters, and the drawing of red herrings across the trail to divert attention from the war, which was then in a most dangerous state, despite some recent victories. Pitt said, "We are engaged in a war for the purpose of defending ourselves against foreign enemies. Is this the reason why we should hazard the consequence of it by distraction at home?" That is more true to-day than it was when he said it away back in 1793. Therefore I hope that for at least the remainder of the war we shall give almost exclusive precedence to matters connected with the war.
Since the minister made his last statement a year ago to the house there has been a vast improvement, so far as his department is concerned. A year ago the war in the Atlantic was in a grave state. It caused many anxious hours not only to the mother country, lest she might be starved out, but to others. The war in the Atlantic was in a most precarious state, and the position was grave. The mother country for centuries has depended upon her supremacy on the seas. But no army, navy or air force could defend them if the merchant marine were inadequate or ceased to function.
The sea is our life, and without in any way deprecating the splendid work that has been done, and will again be done if necessity arises, by our soldiers and our airmen, it is an undeniable fact that any war in which we

War Appropriation-Naval Services
may find ourselves involved against a maritime nation will be won or lost at sea and nowhere else. The greatest menace on the Atlantic during the past year or so undoubtedly has been the U-boat. For a long time the organizers of our defence against this deadly menace ignored the fact that the U-boat could be mastered only by combined operations in the air and on the sea. But the inertia of the higher war direction was at last overcome; the fleet air arm was strengthened, and the admiral commanding and the commodores of the western approaches were given the means to counter this attack. The results are shown by the figures. On November 10, 1943, Mr. Churchill issued an Anglo-American statement to the effect that during August, September and October, 1943, some sixty U-boats had been destroyed. This was mainly on account of the fact that there was unison between the operations on land, sea and in the air. We had land forces in Iceland because we realized that an air base can be held only by an army. The result of all these operations has been that the U-boat has practically retired from the Atlantic.
The figures given on page 17 of the February issue of "Canada at War" show the magnificent achievement of our Canadian merchant marine. I quote some of these figures:

Ottawa	 44,498
Merchant seamen's identification certificates issued	 29,083
In his statement the minister referred to the success achieved in the Mediterannean. I referred the other night, when speaking on the air estimates, to the glorious work of the Royal Navy. I was glad to hear the tribute paid by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) to the Royal Navy and Admiral Cunningham. I have already spoken on these matters but I repeat my remarks to-night. Other matters can be taken up when the various items are before the committee, but in conclusion I should like to refer to one or two matters.
Something should be done, and I hope it will be done before very long, in connection with the adoption of a scheme of national insurance for the three forces. A great deal of economy could be achieved through such a system. Many of our young people are going to be lost in the months to come and we should consider the great losses which the navy has sustained because of lack of proper preparations. A system of national insurance such as they have in the United States would save us a great deal of money, especially in connection with the Department of Pensions
and National Health and the payment of subsistence and other allowances to families after the war.
We had a long statement about the pay and allowances in the three forces, from the heads down. There are still many inequalities, even in the navy. I want to plead the case of the low paid man. We have a citizen army, a citizen navy and a citizen air force. When a man joins the forces there is no reason why he should lose his status as a citizen. Nearly all *these men own property of some kind or another and their investments should be protected. A cost of living bonus should be paid to those men and I hope that these matters are taken up at the proper time.
We are part and parcel of the British empire. On four or five occasions I have called attention to the great need of ports and bases on the Irish sea. Those ports belong to the empire and I hope that this matter will be taken up before very long. I realize that this does not come under the minister's department; it probably belongs in foreign affairs, but the fact remains that New Zealand, Australia and the United States are asking that something should be done. We should have some statement about this. A little while ago I received a letter from Mr. John M. Andrews, formerly Premier of Northern Ireland, in which be referred to the great losses that had occurred through lack of bases and from espionage. He said in part:
The empire must stand together or break up. The neutrality of Eire has been a great disadvantage in this tragic world war and has cost many gallant lives of British and Canadian citizens, as well as those of the United States.
I hope that something will be done to strengthen the hands of the mother country. I hope that something will be done to prevent the giving of signals and tip-offs by spies as was done at the time of Dieppe and Dunkirk. I wish to compliment the minister upon the statement he has given to the committee. Thirty-two thousand men have joined the navy, mostly from the central part of Ontario, and I trust that something will be done immediately about building the new naval barracks at Toronto. The city has provided a site on a waterfront that cost over a million and a *half to fill in behind a retaining wall. This is the second occasion since the last war on which Toronto has provided a site for the navy, the other one being on the waterfront at the foot of Dowling avenue, given for one dollar a year to the Navy League while I was chairman of the harbour board.
I hope that something will be done to provide greater protection for our soldiers, sailors and airmen after the war. These men must

War Appropriation-Naval Services
now be taken through the northern channel on their way to England when we should be able to use the southern channel to Portsmouth and other ports. If we had not had the use of those bases off Eire in the last war we would have lost it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like other speakers who have taken part in this debate I listened with great interest to the review by the minister of the activities of his department. I should like to congratulate him upon the excellence and clarity of his speech, and upon the record of the navy. The record of the Canadian navy in this war is an impressive one and one for which the minister is himself entitled to a great measure of praise. The principal base for the navy is Halifax and any one who has the slightest knowledge of the life of that great port must realize the great task being accomplished by the Canadian navy. As is well known, Halifax is the western terminus of the Atlantic lifeline. It is the control station for the north Atlantic. Throughout the war it has been the outlet for munitions and men. From that port have gone forth great convoys of ships.
One of the most critical phases of the war was the enemy attempt to sink shipping in the Atlantic and prevent our fighting men and supplies from reaching the other side. We have reason to be thankful that that attempt has not met with success. Only a few days ago it was announced that the shipping losses of the allied nations for the month of February were the lowest of any month since 1941. In the defeat of our enemies' attempt to sink shipping and in the successful anti-submarine activities on the Atlantic the Canadian navy took a leading part, the full story of which has not yet been told, It is one in which all Canadians might well take pride.
I wish to express my appreciation of the work done by the Department of National Defence for Naval Services at the dockyard and elsewhere in Halifax and Dartmouth. New buildings have been constructed; improvements and additions have been made, and we now have a thoroughly modern and well equipped naval base. One cannot but be struck with the transformation which has taken place since 1939. I have often thought how much farther we would be advanced to-day' in the task of defeating our enemies if we had had at the outbreak of the war the naval facilities which we now have in Halifax or any substantial part of the navy's present strength in personnel and in ships. The submarine menace would have been much sooner overcome; many precious lives would have been saved, and many valuable ships with their cargoes need not have been lost.

I commend the progressive and far-sighted policy of the navy in acquiring Tribal class destroyers by purchase. It is not without significance that destroyers of this class are designed for offence and not for convoy. Particularly do I commend the government for their decision to build this class of destroyer in Canada. The minister has told us that Tribal class destroyers are the best and fastest afloat. They are heavily armed: They carry as part of their armament 4-7-inch guns. One of this class of destroyer, H.M.C.S. Micmac, was launched at the Halifax shipyards last autumn. I am sure that the many thousands who saw that vessel proceed down the runways into the water must have hoped that she was the forerunner of many more which would be built in Halifax, and that the building of warships will continue to be a permanent and an indestructible industry in the life of that city.
A most important work being carried on by .he navy to-day is the repair of warships and naval craft. It has required the presence in Halifax of many thousands of naval personnel, most of whom are skilled tradesmen. They are engaged in work of the highest priority. It is work which is carried on night and day, seven days a week. The repair facilities of the dockyard and the ship repair yards in Halifax and Dartmouth are taxed to the utmost, and they will, I am sure, continue to be used to full capacity for many years after the war is over.	.
That which is of great interest and importance to the people of Halifax to-day is the continuance of the building of warships after the war. This raises the question of the role of the Royal Canadian Navy in peace time. The navy is now, I understand, constituted of over 250 fighting ships and over 80,000 personnel. Would the minister give the committee some idea what it is anticipated the strength of the navy will be in peace time, and also his view with respect to the continuance of the building of destroyers and other naval craft in Halifax when the war is over? It is true that the war is not yet won; and until it is, our maximum effort must be directed toward its successful and efficient prosecution. The time is come, however, when we are justified in giving some thought to post-war conditions and post-war planning. I realize that money costs and other factors will assume great importance when peace-time estimates for the armed services will be up for consideration in this house. The heavily burdened taxpayer will make his voice heard. I would not want, however, to think there is any possibility of the discontinuance of the building of warships in Halifax or in Canada because of false economy. The industry must

War Appropriation-Naval Services
not be endangered by a policy of centralization. Maritime industries must not have to close up because of their centralization elsewhere for purposes of economy.
I also hope that never again shall we allow our navy and the other armed services to dwindle into insignificance as they did at the termination of the last war. I would expect that a certain measure of navy, army and air force activity will continue in Halifax when the war is over. It will be little short of a calamity if, for instance, our dockyard, now modernized and at a high degree of efficiency, is allowed to fall into disuse.
It is not only the naval facilities of the city of Halifax which have been improved. New buildings have been constructed for army accommodation, and we have not far from the city limits, a well equipped and modern aerodrome which after the war will help to meet expanding air travel requirements.
There is another matter which I wish to bring to the minister's attention. A survey of housing conditions in Halifax has been commenced by E. L. Cousins, wartime administrator for Atlantic ports. He has been studying the problem for months. Questionnaires have been sent out to every man and woman in the city over the age of eighteen. They are asked to answer questions as to their occupation, their length of residence in the city, and also as to whether their wives or husbands are members of the armed services or the merchant marine. It is well known that the acute housing condition has created very difficult conditions in the city of Halifax. It is to the credit of her citizens that they have recognized that this situation has been caused by expanding war activities and that they have accepted it in the proper spirit. Of course there are always some to be found who for political or other purposes attempt to mobilize grievances arising out of these conditions and to capitalize the natural desire of the. people to return after the stress and strain of war to normal life. Happily they are few in number and they succeed in fooling no one but themselves.
Mr. Cousins, when announcing his proposed survey of conditions in Halifax, gave a statement to the press in which, referring to redistribution of population, he said:
The present condition of population congestion had, of necessity, to be dealt with, and in the first instance some relief provided in the form of redistribution of population.
From the viewpoint of prompt relief, the solution of the problem was not to be found in more housing accommodation. The time factor for construction during the winter period, in conjunction with the general material and artisan labour situation, did not permit it, 100-94
therefore it was necessary to request the cooperation of the R.C.A.F. and the army as to their assigning to the navy a portion of their hutment facilities. The rapid but necessary expansion of all the services, particularly the navy, has resulted in serious population congestion in Halifax, Dartmouth and vicinity, and some two months ago there were over 7,000 naval officers and ratings living out of barracks, plus some three thousand dependents in these areas.
As to the R.C.A.F. the number was 1,455, and for the army 1,277.
The R.C.A.F. officials kindly cooperated in turning over the major portion of their "Y" depot quarters to the navy. This transfer was made early in January of this year, with the result that on completion of this movement it will permit of housing some 3,000 officers and men of the navy. The officials of the army are also cooperating to the fullest extent in an endeavour to provide more barrack accommodation for officers and men, also the Merchant Seamen's Pool are cooperating as to the use of a portion of their facilities for general use, so. that in a reasonably short time we should be in the position of providing barrack accommodation for approximately 4,500 officers and men who were previously living out of barracks on subsistence allowance, thereby relieving the rooming-house congestion in both Halifax and Dartmouth.
I think Mr. Cousins' statement makes it clear that the acute housing situation which has developed in Halifax during the last year has in his opinion been occasioned primarily by the rapid expansion of the navy and the fact that arrangements were not made to provide adequate accommodation in Halifax for the greatly increased naval personnel in both officers and ratings.
I do not wish to be understood as passing strictures on those charged with the responsibility of running the navy. I fully realize that warships cannot be held up awaiting repairs, but ,1 would ask the minister whether the transfer of naval personnel of the "Y" depot, and other transfers proposed by Mr. Cousins, will be made and, if so, whether they will solve his housing difficulties in Halifax. I should like to know whether further construction is contemplated for the accommodation of officers and ratings now on subsistence.
The building programme now under way of the armed forces in Halifax is fast nearing completion, so that a supply of skilled labour will soon be available. I should like also to call the minister's attention to one other matter, namely the urgent need in Halifax for restaurant and recreation facilities for members of the services. A large dance hall and canteen is badly needed. Even more urgent is the need of restaurants. The serious situation that existed in Halifax has recently been aggravated through loss by fire of the Knights of Columbus hostel, which I hope



War Appropriation-Naval Services
will soon be replaced on a much larger scale and with much greater dining-room accommodation.
I would ask the minister to cooperate in any way he can in helping the Knights of Columbus war services to get the materials needed to complete the new building and hurry the work through. I realize that the Anzac building has been taken over by the Canadian War Legion services. This building has been remodeled and the Canadian War Legion will soon open a cafeteria. This will improve conditions to some extent but it will not fully meet requirements. I know that the three services are interested in recreation and restaurant facilities, but the navy has the greatest interest because of the very large number of naval personnel now on subsistence in Halifax. I should like the minister to deal with these questions before his estimates are disposed of.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
May I add a word to what has been said as to the growth and development of the navy during these war years. The work they have done in convoying troops as well as food and munitions for the united nations has been remarkable and is something that Canada might well be proud of.
The minister pointed out that the most important obligation is the winning of the war. I suggest that the war may yet be far from won. I have been struck with the figures placed on Hansard, showing that from the most central of the prairie provinces, my own province of Manitoba, there has been an enlistment of over 6,200 officers and ratings. To me it is remarkable that these lads from the prairies should make the efficient sailors that they do. Many of them prior to enlistment had never seen a body of water apart from a prairie slough or creek. A number of these gallant lads from my own constituency have already made the supreme sacrifice.
The minister stated that with respect to those who will return home for demobilization and rehabilitation a directorate has been set up to study the problems of demobilization, rehabilitation and kindred matters and that they wild work with the officers of the other armed services and other departments such as the Department of Pensions and National Health. As I have pointed out on other occasions to the ministers of defence for the army and the air, and as I now suggest to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, many matters regarding those who are discharged from the armed services are still very unsatisfactory. I might mention, for example, clothing allowance. I repeat this, because I think it should be repeated. I assume that those discharged from the navy 
will be granted the same allowance as is given to those from the other armed services. I refer to mustering-out pay and general rehabilitation. May I repeat what I said to the other ministers and express the hope that the present minister, in cooperation with his colleagues, will have some improvement brought about for those under his department who may be discharged.' I submit that something ought to be done to improve matters with regard to clothing allowance, mustering-out pay, general rehabilitation and so on. These and other matters may be brought up under the various items, but I wanted to take this opportunity of saying something with regard to the many gallant youths who have gone into the navy from the prairies and the central part of Canada and who are doing such a fine job.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Many have spoken from all sides of the house on this motion, which is supply for the Royal Canadian Navy. Members who have contributed to the debate come from all over the dominion and I am sure they represent public opinion generally. They all speak in praise and appreciation of the services and achievements of the Royal Canadian Navy. I am sure it must be pleasing to the minister and I think it is a tribute to him, as Minister of Defence for Naval Services, and also to Canada's navy. We in Nova Scotia have always admired ships and the men who go down to the sea. It is a part of our tradition and we meet it in our daily toil. While it would be expected that we would have every appreciation for the navy and its activities in war-time, I think it is most pleasing that it has caught the imagination of the whole of Canada as it has. It shows that we are becoming sea-minded. That will be a good thing for the maritime provinces in the future. Canada will depend upon foreign markets in the future. The sea is the road to the foreign market. The roads must be kept secure and open. While the navy is busily engaged at the present time in defending our shores and contributing to the work of the allied nations in winning victory, I am sure that it will be retained to do a good service when peace comes to this and other nations. Foreign trade depends to a great extent upon the navy. The navy maintains our prestige. It visits foreign ports. It carries our flag into all parts of the world. In the past we have depended upon the British navy. I am sure that Canada has received great benefit from the fact that our navy flew the white ensign and that it was associated with the British navy. But I think the time has come when we must do something for ourselves, and on our own, and I believe that one of the things we

War Appropriation-Naval Services
must be sure of is that Canada will have a substantial navy that is worthy of the traditions and of the efforts of this country in order that we may pursue our foreign trade, which will play such an important part in activities after the war.
It is nice to know that every part of Canada is interested in the navy. We down by the sea are particularly interested because, while the boys come from every part of Canada and every section of the country have contributed a splendid quota to the navy, yet we have the rendezvous of the men and the ships. We see them depart from our shores, and after performing their tour of duty at sea they come back and visit in our ports of Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia in the winter time is the only rendezvous, with the exception of Saint John, New Brunswick, for the Royal Canadian Navy, because of ice conditions on the Atlantic. Because of those conditions the southern and western coast of Nova Scotia is the only place where refitting can be carried on in* the winter time and where the navy can enter and depart without difficulties caused by ice.
The navy must be refitted. I think we are doing a splendid job there in keeping the navy in a fit condition for sea. The refitting of the navy is a highly technical job. A ship is a mechanized machine. It calls into play almost every feature of modern applied science. A ship must be kept in repair and seaworthy. Her power equipment is of many kinds and types. There are different designs and types of engines. The turbine engine, reciprocating engine, diesel engine, internal combustion engine, gasoline engine, the electrical equipment and the armament-all these demand technical skill and properly-trained men to operate and care for them. Then there is the auxiliary equipment, equipment for purposes of intelligence such as asdics, compasses, signals and all the things that go to make the ship an . effective weapon upon the sea. You must also provide for the accommodation of a lot of men. They are placed in rather close quarters on the ship. Their comfort must be looked after. They must be fed. Taken all in all, a ship is a highly technical machine that demands the highest training and men of skill and experience. We have in Nova Scotia at the present time schools where men are trained for the Royal Canadian Navy. I wish to refer particularly to one of those schools, a school that is known as His Majesty's Canadian Ship Cornwallis situate at Deep Brook on the Annapolis basin.
I have heard a lot of talk in this house about good- harbours. We all know that Halifax is a good harbour. We know there are good harbours on the Pacific coast; but I 100-94J
doubt, Mr. Chairman, if there is a place on the Atlantic coast more adaptable or more secure than the place where His Majesty's Canadian Ship Cornwallis is situated It is situate on tidewater just at the foot of the South Mountain in Nova Scotia. It has the South Mountain on one side and the North Mountain on the other side and it is on Annapolis basin, a beautiful sheet of water twenty miles in length, with adequate depth of water, protected on all sides from the sea and free from* ice in the winter time. The entrance to it is through what is known as Digby gut, a narrow neck of water. On both sides of it there is high land easily protected, making secure the naval base. Ships entering Annapolis basin must come up the reaches of the bay of Fundy, with the United States on one side, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick on the other side. The road to Annapolis basin would be a hazardous one for any enemy ship to undertake. I believe that Deep Brook, where His Majesty's Canadian Ship Cornwallis is situate is the most secure from the land, the air and the sea of any place I know of along the Atlantic coast. I am supported in this opinion by men of high naval training, men in the other branches of the services who have given it great consideration.
The places where ships are repaired in Nova Scotia are on the southern coast, and the port of Shelburne, the port of Liverpool, the port of Lunenburg, and the port of Halifax. The training station is across the province on the other side, protected by the equipment on the south shore; and while we on the south shore would have liked to see this station placed nearer to ourselves, I am sure that the navy was wise when they chose Deep Brook as the great naval training station in Nova Scotia. You know, Mr. Chairman, the French came here over two hundred years ago. Champlain and those other great French leaders chose Annapolis basin as their rendezvous when they first came to Canada when the explorers wanted safety. Apparently they knew what they were doing. To-day, at Annapolis, we have Fort Anne, built by the French, which is one of the show places of Nova Scotia. Only a few years ago there was revived what is known as the Order of Good Cheer, patterned after the association set up among the men who were with Champlain at Annapolis, and who passed the long winter evenings in association with each other. That organization has been formed as part of our tourist movement in Nova Scotia, and we invite all Canadians to join it.
I wish to say just a word, Mr. Chairman, about a company of men whom I think deserve the admiration of the people of Canada. A

War Appropriation-Naval Services
few months after the beginning of the war a band of Norwegians came to our shores. As you know, Norway is not a big country but it is a great country. Norwegians have sailed all over the world, and their fishing industry and merchant marine are worthy examples to all other nations. Their whaling fleet was in the south seas when war broke out. Naturally they were not permitted to return to Norway, and the admiralty directed them to the province of Nova Scotia. They first came with their ships to Halifax, but we thought they should be invited to make their headquarters in the port of Lunenburg, the largest commercial fishing centre in Canada, and so they came there and brought their ships with them. The first thing they did was to refit and rearm their ships, which was done in our ports; then they took their place with the Canadian and British navies in protecting the sea routes of the north Atlantic. They opened a training school, to which they brought men from all over Canada and the United States to train for the Norwegian navy. They were with us for nearly three years, during which they built a splendid barracks, which is now used by the Canadian naval service. These men were our fellow citizens for that length of time. They were superior men. They had followed the sea; they knew discipline, and their example was so good that perhaps we were a little envious when they first came to our port. Now they have headquarters in the United States; most of them are at sea and some bare made the supreme sacrifice.
The thought I should like to leave with the minister is that these men were making history for their country while they were in Canada, and in addition, while here, they formed an element in the defence of the coast of Nova Scotia. They were training for service with their own navy; they were more or less outside the circle of things in London and other places where Norwegians received more attention, and it seems to me that something should be done to commemorate their service to Canada and their sojourn in this country. If we have any typically Canadian decoration I think it should be given to those Norwegians, for they earned it by their courage, their discipline and their contribution to this country.
I am sure they enjoyed the hospitality of Nova Scotia, which is made more manifest as a result of the war and because of the admiration we always have for ships and sailors. When we said good-bye to these Norwegians we felt that we were losing good citizens. We believed they were men who would do a good job wherever they went. We hope that ere long 
they may return to their own country, freed from oppression, and help it once more to become a great marine nation.
I want to thank the minister and his department for several things they have done in the last few years that concern the people I represent. The deep-sea fishermen of Nova Scotia go one hundred, two hundred or three hundred miles out to sea. They go east of Newfoundland to the grand banks, the St. Pierre bank, the middle bank and off the coast of Nova Scotia, and they are subject to all the war-time hazards in addition to the hazards of the elements. Our men felt that the submarine danger was so great they were sure to be attacked; and while they were prepared to accept that as one of the hazards of their calling, they thought that to be left alone in a dory three hundred miles out to sea would put them in rather a hopeless position. They came to me, and with the assistance of the minister I was able to get the admiral of the fleet on the east coast to confer with them and arrange for a patrol, so that if they were torpedoed they would know where to find a place of refuge. They were also placed in a restricted area, where they could fish without fear of being run down by the convoys, and our fishermen expressed their great appreciation for the consideration they had been given by the navy. At another time while the navy was operating in St. Margaret's bay, a very deep and spacious body of water west of Halifax, during their training activities they destroyed some of the fishermen's nets. I suppose it was unavoidable, but we brought the matter to the attention of the navy, and they decided that they would so restrict their operations as not to interfere with the shore fishermen. In addition, an undertaking has been given that the nets which were destroyed will be paid for. Some of the fishermen have already been reimbursed for their losses, and I trust that in the near future the others will receive their money so that this spring they may be able to buy new nets in order to carry on their business.
We are also very much interested in the merchant marine. Nothing is too good for it. The merchant marine faces all the dangers that exist today without very much in the way of defence. It is true that these ships have guns with which they may protect, themselves to a certain extent, and I understand that there are two naval men on each ship, but the gun crew is composed of members of the merchant marine. Something has been said here about the merchant marine being forgotten. Well, an order in council was passed which for the first time, in war or in peace, placed the men of the Canadian merchant marine in the same
MARCH 14, 1944	[DOT]
War Appropriation-Naval Services
category as members of the armed forces with regard to pensions and with regard to any disability they might suffer by reason of war activities. May I tell the committee that from my own home town two schooners were sunk in collision because of wartime action. In one collision over twenty men were lost. The Department of Justice interpreted the statute liberally, so that the wives and families of those men are protected, and they are recognized as the dependents of men who have done a splendid service.
There are some who believe that the merchant marine should be put into uniform and be regimented, and they seem to think this would be an' easy thing to do. But we must remember that men of the merchant marine come from every quarter of the world. They are the men who assemble in seaports, wherever there are ships. They go from one port to another; and while I suggest that their services should be recognized, and that we should do anything we can in order to have their services recognized as those of first importance, yet it is difficult in connection with the merchant marine to regiment them the same as we would the personnel of the army, the navy or the air force.
Let me point out, too, that the air force has a considerable marine section. In our part of the country we continually see them in our harbours. We build them and they come there for refitting and reconditioning. The air force has a marine section which is very practicable, and doing a great service along our coast.
When we think of the merchant marine we immediately think of the Navy League. The Navy League of Canada is doing a splendid job for the men of the merchant marine. I am sure anyone who knows Halifax will have seen there the work the league is doing in the interest of seamen, and they will say, "God bless the Navy League." The ditty-bags given to the men at Christmas-time are all provided through the good offices of the Navy League. Our ladies receive letters back from the boys, and some of them say, "Your ditty-bag was the only present we got at Christmas. It was splendid. We thank you for it and we hope that your work will prosper."
In Nova Scotia we have a double duty, because the men of the navy are our guests when their ships come to port for repair. Every vessel must be in port a month to six weeks once every year to have repairs. We know that those boys are receiving a hospitality in keeping with their needs, because our people are most anxious that their morale
and their health shall be sustained both in the interests of our country and of the men themselves. The women along the coast of Nova Scotia work continuously for the navy, the air force and the other services. In my own town the Canadian Legion, a veterans' association, has done splendid work. At that point they have a big hostelry where the men of the navy and the other services are invited to come every night of the week. On Sunday nights they have sing-songs, and they have dances once a week. Ladies of the Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire are continuously working with the Navy League. They make sweaters and socks, and all those comforts the men require. Women's institutes and church organizations in Nova Scotia are contributing their share to the welfare of our men on our coasts. There are dances every week, which are properly chaperoned by the ladies of the town and are under the supervision of naval officers.
I say to the committee that, notwithstanding what has been said about other ports in Canada, down there life is clean and pure, and your boys are in a healthy atmosphere. Their parents can feel that they are well looked after, that they are behaving themselves and that they are a credit to Canada. Lunenburg is a naval base and repair port. Liverpool teems with activity, carrying out repairs for the navy. All hon. members know that Halifax is a great port, where all this work is carried on.
Then, with regard to the navy may I say that much of the work carried on below decks is not spectacular. Much must be done to a ship before she can sail the seas, or take part in that show which we all admire. While we may hear about a vessel when she is at sea, we must realize there are thousands of boys working in the construction and repair shops, and in special services of the navy, who are doing a good job of work. Were it not for them, most certainly the navy could not do its work.
As a member from Nova Scotia I believe I should emphasize the fact that while the navy and industry look after the equipment and refitting of ships, we have a special and personal duty to look after personnel from all parts of Canada who are in our ports. Jack ashore makes a lively scene in our community. There is something about the sea that brings out social characteristics one does not find anywhere else. Comradeship of the sea is generous, and it is liberal. It is international in its aspect. It goes all the way toward those who work on the sea, who face the elements and who fight battles in which there is no quarter. I am sure that down there that

War Appropriation-Naval Services
comradeship is so exemplified and so well carried out that while there might be some question of pollution existing in some of the congested parts of Canada, I can assure the committee that in the ports along the south shore of Nova Scotia life is clean, and everything is as it should be.
When we first started receiving these men from the navy I thought perhaps we were a little extravagant in providing washrooms, toilets and all those things men must have on the waterfronts in order to keep clean. But I changed my mind, because I concluded there is great need; nothing is too good for the health of those men, and we must see to it that they are kept clean and healthy. People come to me and say, "Oh, they are putting linoleums on ships. Look at the extravagance." I want to tell the committee that I have never seen a carpet in an air force or army mess, or a linoleum on a ship that was better than those we have in our homes in the town of Lunenburg. And if we can afford to have them in our homes, then surely the boys who go to sea in congested quarters, boys who are away from their homes and rendering service to their country are entitled to any little comfort they may get when they are off duty, when they are away from danger, or in a place where they may recuperate for the hard days ahead.
We in Nova Scotia are all for the navy because it is part of our life and traditions. We hope that it will be victorious and will continue to carry on. We hope, when peace comes, it will be one of our agents to promote our foreign trade and protect our dignity in other lands, to show the world in after years that Canada is a country that will be great upon the sea.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, coming as I do from the prairies it is always interesting for me to listen to maritimers speak, particularly on a subject about which I am frank to say they do know something. But why should they not know more about shipping, naval affairs and the like than we who come from the prairies? The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley) is an exceptionally enthusiastic maritimer. Before he spoke this evening I asked him how long he expected to be because I was anxious to say just a word or two. He said he would be about fifteen minutes, but I notice that he took nearly forty minutes. However, when he referred to the purity, cleanliness and sweetness of the naval centres in the maritimes I did not mind him going on because so many of our boys and girls from the prairies are down there.

Before this first item passes I should like to take a moment or two to express my admiration for the men and women in the Canadian navy. On March 9 the minister gave us a most interesting review of his department and the Canadian navy. He detailed the part that it has played in the war up to date. All of us have a right to be proud of the facts he set out. We are proud of the most creditable showing the men and women of the Canadian navy are making. Many of these men and women knew nothing about naval affairs, but they joined this service from a sense of patriotism. The minister toid us that when war broke out we had only fifteen ships and some 1,700 men, whereas to-day we have over 600 ships and 75,000 men. He told us that he hoped to get another 12,000 this year, and I have no doubt he will. I know many of the young men and women of the prairies are enlisting in this particular branch of our services.
The minister put on the record the enlistments from the different provinces. Of course Ontario had the banner position, but on the basis of population I think the prairie provinces had a splendid record. Saskatchewan is perhaps the most inland of all provinces. In parts of that province there is not enough water to cover five or ten acres to a sufficient depth to float a rowboat. Many of the boys and girls in that province did not know what a rowboat looked like or whether it was going backward or forward. I am told that when those young men and women from the prairies arrived in Halifax they showed great enthusiasm for the training and made an excellent showing. I am proud to say that some have received commissions. One young man from my own home town is a sublieutenant, and there are many other officers from the prairies. Many of them are in the medical services on hospital ships in the Mediterranean and in every other theatre of war where a naval vessel is to be found.
When the figures of enlistments are broken down I think it will be found that my constituency, perhaps the most inland of any in Canada, has a splendid record. I could give the details of some of those who have enlisted from my home town and tell the committee where they are to-day, but I shall not take the time. Occasionally I meet some of them on the streets of Ottawa in the morning heading toward the naval building. They are fine looking chaps and we are proud of them.
The minister's department paid my constituency a compliment by naming a cargo vessel after a historical point there. Unfortunately that vessel was lost, and I hope that another one will be named after some other

War Appropriation-Naval Services
historical point. On March 9 the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Edwards) made an announcement. As reported on page 1339 of Hansard, he said:
I am particularly pleased this evening-I do not know whether the announcement has been made already, but it will be made to-morrow at the latest-that plans are completed and a contract awarded for the building of the new training ship Tecumseh at Calgary.
That was in his own city. I think he was a little premature in making that announcement because the minister did not confirm it, but he may be a little closer to the inner circles than some of the rest of us. I do not intend to make an announcement about anything that is going to happen in my constituency, [DOT]but on the Qu'Appelle lakes there is open water which I think would be as suitable for a vessel of this type as the city of Calgary.
We have had a lot of discussion on this item. This and the other items are going to pass. In the minister's estimates there is a reduction this year of some $79,000,000, although there are increases in certain items. No doubt there is a good reason for this. We are going to support these items because we are all behind the Canadian navy. We know the part it has played and will have to play in the winning of this war. We know what was done last year and the year before in clearing our coast-line of the submarine menace. We know what has been done in seeing that our merchant ships make a safe landing. I think this is one of the most important branches of our services and it will continue to play a most important part.
In conclusion, I join with other hon. members in praise of our men and women in the navy, and with the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven), who, speaking on March 9, following the minister, put on record a statement, in more detail than I care to do to-night, with respect to enlistments from the prairies and particularly from the district which he represents and which borders on mine. I may say that my constituency extends around the city of Regina, and when he speaks of Regina he is including a number of people from my own district.
