I associate myself with him in expressing admiration of these young men and women from the prairies. They have played and will continue to play an important part in the war. I am sure the minister will have no trouble in getting the men he requires next year. Many of them will come from our district, but I do not want him to take all the boys from the farms; let him leave a few there, because they arp needed. But he wfill get many from the prairies.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
There are
one or two questions I should like to ask the
minister, but may I first join those who have spoken in voicing appreciation of the glowing eulogy which he has paid to the Royal Canadian Navy, and in paying just tribute to the rapid expansion and the courageous and effective record of the naval forces during the present struggle.
I also join hon. members from the prairies in paying a deserved tribute to the boys and girls from that part of the dominion. It might be thought that we on the prairies, including Manitoba, are not especially aware of Canada's navy and of its wonderful record to date in this war; and it would not be surprising, taking into account our geographical position as the central and keystone province of the dominion, if our boys were not navyconscious. But if anyone has any doubt about whether our young people in Manitoba have answered the call of the sea during this war, he should examine the figures stated in the house by the minister on March 9, and to be found in Hansard at page 1309. He there gives the enlistments by provinces from September 1, 1939 to December 31, 1943. Strange as it may seem to the uninitiated, if those figures are compared and related to the population of the provinces according to the 1941 census, it will be found that the record of enlistments in the Royal Canadian Navy from Manitoba surpasses that of every other province, on a percentage basis, except Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There are the merchant marine recruitments in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, too.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
It is a
record to be proud of, and when one considers our geographical position., so far from the eastern and western shores, it is all the more remarkable. It is true that most of our young men and women are in the air force and in the army, and it is natural that they should be. Nevertheless the province as a whole has that splendid record of navy enlistment. Quite a number have joined up from my own constituency; in fact, one of my constitutents, Lieutenant Commander Robert Philip Welland, has been awarded the Distinguished Service Cross. The citation reads: "For courage and enterprise in action against enemy submarines while serving on loan to the Royal Navy." So that the province of Manitoba is enlisting naval men not only in large numbers, but of unsurpassed brains and morale.
I wish to thank the minister for having personally looked into and corrected the matter of income tax rates for a certain class of naval officers, one of them from my constituency.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
The training given boys in the navy is undoubtedly of a high order. When I was speaking the other day to a vocational training man of high standard who has conducted and observed the work of trades training in all the services, he gave it as his opinion that the navy training in trades was unsurpassed. I understand that the complete training programme is equally good.
The question I wish to leave with the minister is -this. In some countries, all young men have to do a certain amount of military training. Some people in Canada are looking forward to that very thing after the war Has the minister given any consideration to having all young men in this dominion undertake a certain amount of naval training in peace time?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Does the minister intend to reply to some of the points raised and the questions asked?

War Appropriation-Naval Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Before the minister replies, I should like to say just a word or two. I have listened with a great deal of pleasure and pride to all hon. members who have taken part in this discussion as they have pointed to the achievements of men from their own parts of the country and the magnificent effort those men have made as members of our Canadian navy. I would be remiss if I did not call the attention of the committee to the fact that my own constituency has the honour of having produced Vice-Admiral Nelles, the man who is responsible for the'Splendid work our navy has done. I thought it was only within my rights, while others were emphasizing the great contribution that has been made by men from their own constituencies, that I should point out that the vice-admiral of our splendid navy comes from my own district, where he was born.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I may answer nowr some of the questions that have been asked in the last few days and I shall endeavour to answer them in the order in which they were put. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) wished to know how many men would want to retire from the navy at the. end of the war. It is difficult to say at this moment how many men will wish to retire and how many men the navy may have permanently after the war. The present authorized complement of the Royal Canadian Navy, post-war, is between 8,000 and 9,000. That complement was authorized in 1941. That is the post-war complement, and various plans have been brought up by the staff at different times, suggesting other possible maxima and minima complements, but I am not able to say at this time what the post-war complement will be.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Since then two cruisers have been announced and two aeroplane carriers.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Yes. I hope, as many hon. gentlemen have hoped, that the complement will be reasonably adequate for a country the size of Canada and for the duties which the Canadian navy may be called upon to perform.
My hon. friend went on to ask whether the navy would take part in the Pacific war. That question is covered by the general statement made by the Prime Minister, that we were all in the war together as united nations and would all pursue it to the end. The Canadian navy, I should think, would play a part in the war against Japan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
If I may interrupt for a moment, there was another question with re-100-95
gard to rehabilitation, whether the minister plans to have training courses, or whether they will come in under the pensions and national health training scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That was another question asked by my hon. friend, whether the navy intended to have training classes for itself alone, as I understand, or its demobilized men, I assume-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: For those about to be demobilized and desiring training, or whether they would come under pensions and national health.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Of course, any training of men after they are demobilized will have to come under the Department of Pensions and National Health. As to the training of men before demobilization, I think I can say to my hon. friend that at the present time practically the entire effort of the navy is directed to the winning of the. war. Forty per cent of the men are at sea, and in the type of ship we have, the smaller ship, there is not a very great opportunity for these men to take any courses of an educational nature beyond, of course, such training as they may acquire in the ordinary course of their duties. When the pressure of training eases, it is our hope that we can use a certain amount of the time, of some of the men at least, in training them for the postwar period. In that step we shall cooperate with the Department of Pensions and National Health, the Canadian Legion and those other groups that are interesting themselves in the educational welfare of the men of the armed services. We also plan, when we can spare the personnel from present operational duties, to institute a programme of vocational guidance or counselling for our men. I think I said the other night that we had a directorate of demobilization and at the head of it we had a reserve officer. We thought that would be the proper branch of the service from which to select an officer for such a task, because practically all the men demobilized will be from the reserve. This officer is at present out of Ottawa, proceeding around from place to place, talking to officers and ratings, endeavouring to study their problems and bring back to us suggestions for their solution.
My hon. friend asked whether entry in the R.C.N.-that is the permanent branch of the service-was now made from the volunteer reserve division, or whether there was any direct entry into the R.C.N. I may tell him that a man can come into the R.C.N. either directly or through the volunteer reserve



War Appropriation-Naval Services
division- My hon. friend then spoke about an advertisement which he had seen calling for certain types of ratings in the navy, namely, stokers and communication ratings. He wanted to know whether any others were needed. I would say to my hon. friend, yes. there are others needed, but the great need is for cooks, stewards, stokers and communication ratings. As I intimated to the house the other day, we plan to take into the navy in the next fiscal year some 12,000 personnel of all classes. That would include, of course, some ordinary seamen. Sometimes we need a certain type of rating and at other times another; and when we fill up the need we stop recruiting in that particular category. At the moment, however, cooks, stewards, communication .ratings and stokers are the types of ratings we need most.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Are they coming forward in satisfactory numbers?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
They are coming forward in reasonably good numbers, yes. We have to advertise for some of them and the divisions are constantly on the look-out for the types of men needed. [DOT]
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) paid a well deserved tribute to the Navy League for its work. He paid a tribute to the founders of the league in this country, such as the late Sam Harris, Aemilius Jarvis and the present head of the navy, D. H. Gibson. With all that I agree. My hon. friend then wanted to know whether we were training Canadians to fly off aircraft carriers; that if we were to have carriers Canadians should be trained to fly off them. On that point I may -say to my hon. friend that we have not yet established a branch of what is called in Britain the fleet air arm, but there are certain Canadians who are doing naval flying in Great Britain. There has been an organization in Halifax known as H.M.S. Canada which did some recruiting of Canadians for the fleet air arm of the Royal Navy. Some seventy-six Canadians have gone into the Royal Naval Fleet Air Arm through H.M.S. Canada. There is also another way of getting into the fleet air arm, and that is by an arrangement under which we have agreed to lend to them a limited number of R.C.N.Y.R. officers for training and employment in air duties. We have agreed to give them thirty-two pilots, twenty-five observers and fifteen air engineer officers. These officers are already in the Canadian naval service or they will be taken into the service of the Canadian navy and then lent to the Royal Navy.
IMr. A. L. Macdonald.]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Before the minister leaves the fleet air arm possibilities, may I ask a question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The minister stated that some seventy-six young Canadians are being trained for the fleet air arm of the Royal Navy. At the present time some are being trained in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No doubt, yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Where are they going
after they are trained?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: They would go back to the Royal Navy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: If, later on, Canada finds it necessary to have aircraft carriers is it possible that those young Canadians will be brought back?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I
would hope that that might take place, yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: While they are in the Royal Navy, are they paid according to the Royal Navy standard, or is their pay supplemented by the difference between the Canadian rate and the British rate?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: As to those men who enter the Canadian navy and are then lent to the British navy, they would continue at the Canadian rate of pay, but I should assume that a man who joined the British navy directly, without going through the Canadian navy, would receive the British rate of pay just the same as a Canadian who went over to England before the war and joined the Royal Air Force. He is a member of the Royal Air Force and would get Royal Air Force pay.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: When I asked the question before, I understood that the minister answered it by saying that they would be taken care of in every way, the same as if they had joined the Canadian service. Apparently that is not the case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Those who joined the Royal Navy directly from here without passing through the Canadian navy would not be under our control. We would have no control over them, and I should assume that they would get-I shall look into the matter and make sure of it by to-morrow -Royal Navy rates of pay.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I am informed that the
pay is much smaller than if they were in the Canadian navy; but with regard to the seventy-six mentioned by the minister, may I

War Appropriation-Naval Services
say they were all young lads, mostly university students. What I cannot get into my head is how they got into the fleet air arm department. I do not know whether they tried to enlist in Canada; but I believe they were all too young; at least I know some of them were too young to be admitted into the Canadian navy. In some way or other, however, they were enlisted into the Royal Air Force. How did that happen?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There are, as the Minister for Air said in his speech several times, a good many Canadians in the Royal Air Force, Canadians who went directly into the Royal Air Force. Some of them went over before the war; some of them went over shortly after the war and joined the Royal Air Force directly. They stand in exactly the same position as a native of Britain would stand in that air force, I should think. They would be paid the British rates of pay. The same thing applies to those in the fleet air arm. If a Canadian, of his own accord, went to England and joined that branch of the service, without ever going through the Canadian navy, I think he would receive the British rate of pay, because we would have no control or jurisdiction over that person.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: As I understand it, these young lads did not go to England to join the fleet air arm; somebody, either from England or representing the British Government in Canada, enlisted these young men directly out of university schools just a year ago, two or three years after the war broke out.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
If
*they enlisted directly from Canada they never passed through Canadian hands at all, so that I should think it would be very difficult for us to try to follow them and give them Canadian rates of pay. To begin with, we would not know who they were; we would have no record of them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I am trying to find out
by what method someone from Great Britain, or someone in Canada representing Great Britain, got these young lads out of the university schools.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I
am afraid I am not making myself very clear, but this is the .memorandum I xhave here. In the early days of the war, before the United States entered it, Admiral Bonham-Carter looked after the entry of Canadians who wanted to join the Royal Navy Fleet Air Arm. That was the beginning of the arrangement under which Canadians joined that branch of 100-951
the service. It is estimated that some seventy-six Canadians have entered the Royal Navy for air duties. These men who joined the fleet air arm- of the Royal Navy directly from civilian life would, I should think, have to accept the ordinary pay and other arrangements of the service which they joined. I do not think there is any question about that. I may tell my hon. friend, however, that some of those officers and ratings who joined the Royal Naval Air Service have since expressed a desire to transfer to the Royal Canadian Navy, and in some cases that has been done; they have come back and attached themselves to the Canadian navy. If, however, they have not done that, they will have to take British rates of pay, having joined a British service directly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I appreciate very much
*the courtesy of the minister, but the matter still is not clear in my mind. The minister speaks of a time prior to that which I have in mind. The young lads to whom I refer were taken into the fleet air arm within, the last year or thereabouts. A number of them were attending schools in Toronto and elsewhere, and I am trying to find out how some authorities outside Canada could come into this country in 1943 and enlist these young men from our universities. Undoubtedly these lads wanted to join the fleet air arm, but I should like to know how it happened that they were taken right from under our very noses, one might say, and enlisted in the fleet air arm. Perhaps they might have been enlisted in our own air force.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
As
my hon. friend knows, in addition to this group of men to whom I have referred, some two thousand Canadian officers and; ratings are serving with the British navy on loan at the present time, so that it is not unusual for our people to find their way into the British navy. There was a period, though I am not sure just how long it lasted, in the early days of the war when the British wanted us to enlist certain types of young men for them; skilled radio men, for instance. Young men with a high degree of scientific skill and training in our universities were very much sought after by the British, and we allowed a certain number of them to be enlisted in that way in order to help the British meet the great problems facing them at that time. If my hon. friend would give me the dates he has in mind, the last dates on which this enlisting took place, I would be able to tell more definitely, but the total number involved, according to my figures, is only seventy-six who have gone in this way since the beginning.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Into the fleet air arm?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes, directly into the fleet air arm.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Does that include the number who were enlisted last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is the number given me up to date. In addition, as I told my hon. friend, some others have gone in from the Canadian navy. We have a full record of those men; we know who they are and we know the number we are to furnish. We are to supply some seventy-two in all. They pass through our own divisions and establishments, and we know all about them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I shall obtain more particulars and give the minister the information. Then he may be able to tell me what I am trying to find out, for I am afraid I have not secured the information in what I have been told so far.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Very well.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Are these young men who are enlisted in the fleet air arm trained in Canada or sent to England for training? I believe a number of these men are being trained in this country, though I am not sure whether they are Canadian or English boys.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I think there is some preliminary training done here for the fleet air arm. Kingston is one place where it is carried on, I think, and Aylmer is another; but the advanced training would have to be done outside Canada, some in England and some in the United States.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Then any Canadian boys who enlist in the fleet air arm would be partly trained in Canada before leaving?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes, they may be trained here; it would depend upon where the British would want to send them. Probably most of them would be trained here.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Would the minister explain why Canada is not acquiring the two aircraft carriers, just as she is acquiring the two cruisers? Apparently we are merely manning the two aircraft carriers, and the ships and planes will still belong to Great Britain, while the pilots who fly those planes are to come from Great Britain, according to the minister's statement of March 9. Would he explain why we are not acquiring the ships and why we cannot man them completely?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The question of acquiring the ships is bound up

with the whole question of lend-lease. That is a complicated and intricate business which would take a long time to explain. That is why we have not acquired the ships outright. The cruisers we are acquiring are British ships, built in Great Britain and controlled by the admiralty. They can do what they wish with them, but the aircraft carriers in question are not in that position. They were built in the United States and acquired by Great Britain, and then they were turned over to us. As I say, it is a matter in which the three countries are involved, and at the time this seemed to be the only arrangement we could make. However, the matter is still under consideration and it. is possible that some change may yet be made in that arrangement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is it hoped that eventually Canada will acquire the two aircraft carriers?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I would hope that we might, but, as I say, we cannot acquire them without the consent of the other parties to the bargain; we have to secure that first,.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Why can we not supply the pilots?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I do not think we have enough Canadian pilots to operate those two carriers. We might, by scouring the whole British fleet air arm, get enough. But I hope that some of the pilots which the British will put on those ships will be Canadians serving with that branch who, I am sure, would be glad to serve alongside Canadian naval officers.
The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) raised a question about the acoustic torpedo, and recent developments in German methods of attack. He praised the admiralty for the speed with which they had instituted counter measures against the acoustic torpedo. May I tell the committee that the Canadian navy has a scientific research branch which has been most active in this very field, andi which had anticipated and had begun studies before the attacks were made by the acoustic torpedo. Although this is the sort of subject which one cannot discuss in complete detail, I think I can say that the information given by our scientists to the admiralty was of considerable value in the establishment of these counter measures. I might say, too, that immediately the attack by the acoustic torpedo was made, an officer was flown from Canada to England to ensure that there would be a complete interchange of information between our department here and the admiralty. The result of this cooperation has been highly gratifying.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) asked if we were going to build carriers in this country for our navy. The answer to that is that there is no intention at the present time of doing so.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) raised the question as to why the pay for women in the services was not equal to the pay for men, and ventured the hope that I would be able to be more generous than my colleagues in the two other services had been. The arrangements in the services are the same, namely the basic pay of women is eighty per cent of that of men. But the trades pay is the same. In the United States I understand the basic pay for women is exactly the same, while in Great Britain I believe it is two-thirds of that received by the men. So that we are in between the American and British systems.
My hon. friend wants to know why there is not equal pay for women. I do not know whether my colleagues have given these reasons, but the chief reason assigned for the difference in pay is that normally women are not employed in active combatant positions, nor are they trained for combat. In the strict sense, therefore, women cannot be said completely to replace fighting men.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: But of course there are some men who are not fighting men.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is true, and that is the argument made against what I have said. But the point is that every man is liable to go on active service. Even such men as paymasters, while employed at one point in one week, may in the next week be aboard ships on active service. The same applies to doctors, special branch officers and so on. Everyone is on active service and liable to be placed in a zone of danger. It would be difficult to divide the men to a point where we could say that one man is combatant-and another is not. I am giving the reasons which have been given to me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I imagine the minister is like me in that respect; probably he is pretty hard to convince.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It might have been simpler from the beginning to have given them all the same rate of pay.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I think they should have it, really.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
But there it stands, in that position. I do not wholly defend the discrimination against women, because there are many women working for us in clerical positions, women doing the work of coders, cipherers, signallers, and the like, who are certainly doing their work
just as well as it would be done by men. They are quite equal to men, and it is a hardship on them that they do not receive the same pay as do men working opposite them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Has there been a conference between the army, air force and navy officials respecting this matter? I think I see a more sympathetic glint in the minister's eye than I found in the case of the two other ministers who have charge of the other defence departments.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Perhaps just a touch of chivalry.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Perhaps through his good offices he might persuade the other two. I believe I can see much more sympathy in the minister's atitude than I have seen thus far in the debate. My suggestion would be that when we have got this far perhaps we might go a little farther.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is a matter which would have to be settled by the three services. I would not, and neither would my colleagues, think of adopting a different scale of pay from that in the other services. But the matter has been considered at great length. We began, I believe, at the British rate of two-thirds, and we raised it to four-fifths. With good luck and generous hearts it might be that we would go even a little farther. But I cannot assure my hon. friend, still less members of the women's services, that that would happen. However, some progress has been made in the past, and it may be that more can be made in the future.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I understand the door is not definitely closed, then.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Where I am concerned, the door is never closed. All these matters can be reconsidered.
The hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross), inquired whether the ship Toronto had been, commissioned. The answer is that that good ship is not yet in commission, but that she will be this year.'

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Since speaking about an hour ago I have been informed by the hon. member for Yale that an announcement was made to-day to the effect that a ship has been named the Qu'Appelle. I refrained from speaking at length when I spoke before, but I wonder if the minister would inform the committee as to the type of ship, and the reason for naming it thus? I believe the announcement was made in the radio news at one o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
My hon. friend referred to the Fort Qu'Appelle, which was sunk?

War Appropriation-Naval Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I
shall give an answer before the committee rises, and shall ascertain that there is no confusion between names.
The hon. member for St. Paul's asked about Canadians serving with the Royal Navy and inquired whether they would receive pensions at Canadian rates. The Pension Act provides in effect that where the British act does not meet the case, full pensions will be paid by Canada. What we do is to make up the difference between the British rate of pension and the Canadian rate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is it proposed to have the service chevrons now used by the army adopted by the navy as well?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I believe' the regulation applies to all three services. I do not know that the navy was greatly in favour of the business, but they are entitled to wear chevrons.
The junior member for Halifax (Mr. Macdonald) raised the question about the role the Canadian navy would play in peace and what strength the navy would be. I believe I answered his questions when dealing with certain matters raised by the hon. member for Yale.
The hon. member then went on to ask whether destroyers would be built in Halifax and expressed the hope that this would be done after the war. Of course these post-war plans and projects are difficult to assess with accuracy at this time, but I can say that if there is to be a Canadian navy in the postwar period, there should be destroyers. I think the destroyer is the heart of the navy; whatever other type of ship you have or have not, you must have destroyers. I think they should be built in this country. There has been some criticism of the cost of building these destroyers in Halifax. Undoubtedly it has been greater than the cost in Great Britain, but these were the first two to be built in Canada and then Canada's wage rates are somewhat higher than those of Great Britain. However, I do not think we could ever hope to develop a navy in this country unless we Resorted to our own shipbuilding facilities for at least the greater number of the ships in that navy. I should think that destroyers will be built in Canada as long as there is a Canadian navy. Halifax seems to be the logical place for the building of destroyers. They have to put in there for repairs and refits, and in the winter months many other ports are denied to them. It seems to have the proper combination of building and repair facilities.
fMr. A. L. Macdonald.)
The hon. member made some inquiry about the transfer of naval personnel to the former air force barracks at Halifax. I am able to tell him that the transfer is proceeding and it has been found to be very helpful. I understand some 2,000 naval personnel have been transferred and this will help to relieve congestion in the city. My hon. friend wanted to know if we contemplated any additional building in Halifax. In the past, building in Halifax has been difficult on account of the great shortage of labour, and at the moment we have not in contemplation the building of any new barracks. Undoubtedly restaurant and recreation facilities are greatly needed, and I shall be glad to do anything I can to assist or to strengthen the hands of the auxiliary services and those others who are interested in the matter.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) referred to the freighter which unfortunately was lost, but I am glad to be able to say to him that there is a fine destroyer
called the Qu'Appelle which we have acquired from the British navy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I asked about the naval disposal committee.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: My hon. friend's question was about the arrangements made for salvage and disposal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I wanted more details about naval order 3444. I wished to know whether tenders were called for.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There is at naval headquarters a disposal committee, of which one of the officers of the stores branch is the chairman. At each base there is a subcommittee which deals with the question of salvage and disposal and which reports to the headquarters committee. My hon. friend wanted to know why they had to refer matters to headquarters.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I
wanted to know if tenders were called for in connection with the disposal of these goods, and I should also like to know just what is disposed of. Would this not come under the new disposal committee set up under munitions and supply?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
It does. The fact is that the naval services disposal committee authorized by naval order 3444 is a collecting body to determine what assets are surplus to our requirements. The chairman of that committee is the deputy chief of naval equipment and supply, Mr. L. C. Thompson, who was formerly manager of

Mexico Embassy
stores, Canadian National Railways. This committee is made up of representatives of all the branches which have anything to do with buildings or properties or ships or naval ordnance or stores of any description. At each base there is a small counterpart set up. The naval services disposal committee is not empowered to effect any sale of surplus assets; this must be done by the committee under the jurisdiction of the Department of Munitions and Supply. The committee of which Mr. Thompson is chairman reports any surplus through the deputy minister to the crown assets allocation committee, after having first offered the surplus to the army and air force. It often happens that a thing which is surplus -with us is needed by the other services. Similarly, the local committees of other places have no power to dispose of surplus assets by tender or otherwise.

should like to ask a few more questions.
